Double Time Pay: Twice Your Rate — and Federal Law Never Requires It

Direct AnswerDouble time pays 2× your hourly rate, but federal law never requires it. Learn when it applies, how to calculate it, and see worked examples at $25 an hour.

Gross pay estimates
By Saahil•Published October 29, 2026•9 min read•Overtime & Paycheck Guides
A closer look

In this guide

The Short AnswerWhat Is Double Time Pay?When Do You Actually Get Double Time?The Double Time FormulaDouble Time, Worked Step by StepStraight Time vs Time and a Half vs Double TimeDouble Time After Federal TaxesHow to Use the Overtime CalculatorLimitationsFrequently Asked QuestionsKey Takeaways & Action Plan

Use your actual work schedule for a more useful estimate.

Quick Answer

Double time pays exactly twice your regular hourly rate — at $25 an hour, every double-time hour pays $50. But no federal law ever requires it: the Fair Labor Standards Act caps required overtime at 1.5×. Double time reaches a paycheck only through a state law such as California's daily rules, a union contract, or an employer's own written policy.

The Short Answer

The arithmetic is the easy part: double-time rate = your regular rate × 2. Earn $25 an hour and your double-time rate is $50; work 8 hours at that rate and you have earned $400 for those hours alone. In a week of 40 regular hours plus 8 double-time hours, the gross is $1,000 + $400 = $1,400.

The hard part is entitlement. Whether any of your hours are paid at 2× depends entirely on which rule covers your job — a state statute, a collective bargaining agreement, or a line in your employer's handbook. The most common misunderstanding in American payroll sits right here: working on a holiday, a weekend, or at night earns no premium at all under federal law. If double time shows up on your check, some written rule put it there. This guide works through the math first, then the rules that grant it, then what is left after federal taxes.

What Is Double Time Pay?

Double time is a premium pay rate equal to two times an employee's regular hourly rate, paid for specific hours that a law, contract, or policy singles out — typically extremely long days, a seventh consecutive day of work, or designated holidays. It sits at the top of the three standard premium tiers:

  • Straight time (1×): your regular rate, for hours up to the first premium threshold.
  • Time and a half (1.5×): the federal overtime standard for non-exempt hours past 40 in a workweek.
  • Double time (2×): the top tier — never federally required, granted only by state law, contract, or policy.

Every double-time calculation has three inputs, and getting any one of them wrong changes the answer:

  1. Your regular rate. This is not always your base wage. Under federal rules, the regular rate folds in non-discretionary bonuses and shift differentials. Example: a $24 base wage plus a $52 non-discretionary bonus in a 52-hour week adds $52 ÷ 52 = $1 an hour, making the regular rate $25 — so the double-time rate is $50, not $48.
  2. Your double-time hours. Only the hours past the trigger earn 2×, never the whole shift. In California, hour 13 of a day is double time; hours 1–8 are straight time and hours 9–12 are time and a half.
  3. The rule that grants it. A statute, a contract, or a written policy. No rule, no double time — however long the shift felt.

On a pay stub, double-time hours appear as their own earnings line with their own rate, separate from regular and overtime lines. Our pay stub guide shows where each premium line sits and how to check it against your hours.

When Do You Actually Get Double Time?

Double time comes through exactly three doors. They are listed here in order of how binding they are — a statute binds every covered employer, while a policy binds only the employer who wrote it.

1. California law

California is the only state that mandates double time statewide, under Labor Code §510. Two triggers:

  • Hours past 12 in a workday are paid at 2×. (Hours 9–12 that day pay 1.5×.)
  • Hours past 8 on the seventh consecutive day of work in one workweek are paid at 2×. The first 8 hours that day pay 1.5× — even if the week's total hours are unremarkable.

Seventh-day example at $20 an hour, 10 hours worked on day seven: 8 × $30 (time and a half) + 2 × $40 (double time) = $240 + $80 = $320, against $200 at straight time. Two cautions: a "workday" and a "workweek" are consecutive 24-hour and 7-day periods your employer defines, and the seventh day means seven consecutive days inside one workweek — a streak that straddles two workweeks does not trigger it.

2. Other state daily-overtime rules (at 1.5×, not 2×)

A few states count the day as well as the week, but pay the premium at time and a half: Alaska past 8 hours in a day, Colorado past 12 in a day, Nevada past 8 in a day for lower-wage workers, and Oregon past 10 in a day for manufacturing employees. No other state mandates 2× statewide; Puerto Rico separately requires double time for work on statutory rest days. The full state-by-state map is on our overtime rules by state page.

3. Union contracts and employer policy

Most double time in the United States arrives this way. Collective bargaining agreements in healthcare, emergency services, utilities, and manufacturing commonly promise 2× for holidays, for hours past a daily cap, or for a seventh day. Many non-union employers copy the pattern voluntarily for holiday shifts, because a 2× shift is easier to staff than a 1× one. Either way, the written document is the entitlement: if the handbook promises double time for a worked holiday, you are owed it; if it does not, the holiday itself creates no right to it.

What federal law says instead

The Fair Labor Standards Act requires non-exempt employees to be paid at least 1.5× the regular rate for hours past 40 in a workweek — and stops there. It has no daily trigger, no 2× tier, and no premium for holidays, weekends, or nights. Salaried exempt employees are outside the federal premium rules entirely. When a state rule and the federal rule both cover the same hour, the one that pays the employee more is the one that applies.

The Double Time Formula

Three short formulas cover every case in this guide:

Double-Time Rate = Regular Rate × 2

Double-Time Pay = Double-Time Rate × Double-Time Hours
Total Pay = Regular Pay + Time-and-a-Half Pay + Double-Time Pay

The double-time rate for common wages, and what a full 8-hour double-time shift pays at each:

Regular rateDouble-time rate (2×)8 double-time hours
$15.00$30.00$240.00
$17.00$34.00$272.00
$20.00$40.00$320.00
$25.00$50.00$400.00
$30.00$60.00$480.00
$35.00$70.00$560.00
$40.00$80.00$640.00

Figure 1: Double-time rates for common wages. Eight hours is the standard holiday shift — the most common block of double time in policy-based workplaces.

Double Time, Worked Step by Step

Example 1 — a holiday week at $25 an hour. Your employer's written policy pays double time for hours worked on a company holiday. In one week you work 40 regular hours, 8 of them on the holiday itself:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Regular pay40 hours × $25$1,000.00 per week
Step 2 — Double-time rate$25 × 2$50.00 per hour
Step 3 — Double-time pay8 hours × $50$400.00 per week
Step 4 — Weekly total$1,000 + $400$1,400.00 per week
Annual total (if weekly)$1,400 × 52$72,800.00

Of that annual figure, $20,800 is double-time pay and $52,000 is regular pay. Honesty note: the annual line assumes the pattern repeats every week, which is rare — double time usually clusters on holidays and peak weeks. If your policy produces two such weeks a year, the honest annual addition is 2 × $400 = $800 of double-time pay, not $20,800.

Example 2 — a 14-hour California day at $20 an hour. One workday crosses all three tiers:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — First 8 hours (straight time)8 hours × $20$160.00
Step 2 — Hours 9–12 (time and a half)4 hours × $30$120.00
Step 3 — Hours 13–14 (double time)2 hours × $40$80.00
Day total$160 + $120 + $80$360.00

The same 14 hours at a flat $20 would pay $280, so the two premium tiers add $80 to the day. Only the last two hours earn double time — a useful check if a stub ever shows the whole day at 2×, or none of it. Our Overtime Calculator reproduces this exact day with its CA-style daily rule, shown step by step in the How to Use section below.

Straight Time vs Time and a Half vs Double Time

The same hours at the three tiers, at $25 an hour — 40 regular hours plus 10 additional hours in one week:

How the 10 extra hours are paidRatePay for the 10 hoursWeekly totalWhere the rate comes from
Straight time (no premium rule reaches them)$25.00$250.00$1,250.00Hours under every threshold
Time and a half$37.50$375.00$1,375.00Federal law, past 40 hours a week
Double time$50.00$500.00$1,500.00California law, a contract, or a policy

Figure 2: Ten premium hours at $25 an hour. Double time beats time and a half by $125 on those hours — $12.50 an hour.

One rule prevents a common payroll error: premiums never stack on the same hour. An hour is paid once, at the highest rate that applies to it. You do not collect 1.5× and then 2× on top, and California's daily and weekly premiums do not pyramid the same hour twice either. For the standard 1.5× case on your own numbers, the Time and a Half Calculator fixes the multiplier so there is nothing to mis-set.

Double Time After Federal Taxes

Double-time pay is taxed exactly like regular pay — the same brackets and the same 7.65% FICA. Our overtime tax guide explains why a bigger check can still be withheld at a higher pace: payroll annualizes the check, and the difference settles when you file. For a single filer in 2026 taking the standard deduction, here is Example 1's $72,800 year after federal taxes only — state tax, 401(k), and health premiums are excluded, so a real paycheck lands lower:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Gross pay40 regular + 8 double-time hours, weekly, × 52$72,800.00
Step 2 — Standard deductionSingle filer, 2026− $16,100.00
Step 3 — Taxable income$72,800 − $16,100$56,700.00
Step 4 — Federal income tax10% × $12,400 + 12% × $38,000 + 22% × $6,300$7,186.00
Step 5 — FICA$72,800 × 7.65% (SS $4,513.60 + Medicare $1,055.60)$5,569.20
Take-home (federal only)$72,800 − $7,186 − $5,569.20$60,044.80

That is $5,003.73 a month on average, or $2,309.42 per biweekly paycheck, before state tax. The marginal bracket is 22%, but the effective federal rate is only 9.9% ($7,186 ÷ $72,800), because the first dollars are taxed at 10% and 12%. The FICA line uses the same 7.65% broken down in our FICA guide.

Honesty note: this sketch assumes all $72,800 counts as wages for both income tax and FICA, with no pre-tax deductions — and it inherits Example 1's every-week assumption. Scale it to your own pattern: taxes follow your actual annual gross, whatever mix of straight, 1.5×, and 2× hours produced it.

  3. Step 3 — Set the multiplier to 2×: choose "2× · double time" in the Overtime multiplier select, or tap the "2× Double time" preset button.

  5. Step 5 — Read the receipt panel: your double-time rate, weekly overtime pay, and the annual totals, with the formula shown next to the result.

Limitations

Keep these limits in mind before relying on any figure above:

  1. State coverage: California's §510 rules are the only statewide 2× mandate covered in depth. Other states' daily rules pay 1.5× and carry their own exceptions — check your state on the overtime rules by state page before assuming a premium.
  2. Regular rate: the examples treat the base wage as the regular rate. Non-discretionary bonuses and shift differentials raise the regular rate, which raises every premium figure with it.
  3. Policy-based double time: where double time comes from a handbook or contract, that document controls — this article cannot read it, and unwritten practice generally is not an entitlement.
  4. Exempt status: salaried exempt employees sit outside these premium rules entirely unless a contract or policy says otherwise.
  5. Tax sketch: federal only, single filer, standard deduction, no credits or pre-tax deductions. State income tax would reduce take-home further.
  6. Not legal or tax advice: entitlement disputes turn on your employer's defined workweek, your schedule records, and your documents. A state labor agency or an employment attorney is the right next step for a specific claim.

Frequently Asked Questions

The questions readers ask most about double time:

What is double time pay?

Double time is pay at exactly twice your regular hourly rate. At $25 an hour, your double-time rate is $50 an hour, so 8 double-time hours pay $400 on top of your regular pay. It is the highest of the three standard pay tiers: straight time (1×), time and a half (1.5×), and double time (2×).

Is double time required by federal law?

No. The Fair Labor Standards Act requires only time and a half (1.5×) for non-exempt hours past 40 in a workweek, and it never requires 2× pay, daily overtime, or holiday premiums. Double time exists only where a state law such as California's, a union contract, or an employer's own written policy grants it.

How do I calculate double time pay?

Multiply your regular rate by 2 to get your double-time rate, then multiply by the number of double-time hours, then add your regular pay. At $25 an hour with 8 double-time hours: $25 × 2 = $50 per hour, $50 × 8 = $400 of double-time pay, and $1,000 of regular pay for 40 hours — a $1,400 week before taxes.

When does California require double time?

In two situations: every hour past 12 in a single workday, and every hour past 8 on the seventh consecutive day of work within one workweek (the first 8 hours that day pay time and a half). Only the hours past the trigger earn 2× — the rest of the day is paid at straight time or time and a half.

What is double time for $25 an hour?

It is $50 an hour. A full 8-hour double-time shift pays $400, and a week of 40 regular hours plus 8 double-time hours pays $1,400 gross. At time and a half instead, those same 8 hours would pay $37.50 an hour — $100 less across the shift.

Is double time taxed at a higher rate?

No. Double-time pay is ordinary wages: the same federal brackets and the same 7.65% FICA apply as to any other hour you work. A larger check can be withheld at a higher pace because payroll annualizes it, but the difference settles when you file your return — there is no separate double-time tax.

Key Takeaways & Action Plan

  • Double time = regular rate × 2, paid only on the hours past a trigger — at $25 an hour, each double-time hour pays $50.
  • Federal law never requires it. The FLSA stops at 1.5× past 40 hours a week; 2× comes only from California law, a union contract, or a written employer policy.
  • California's triggers are daily: hours past 12 in a workday, and hours past 8 on the seventh consecutive day of a workweek.
  • Premiums never stack on the same hour — each hour is paid once, at the highest rate that applies to it.
  • It is taxed as ordinary wages — on a $72,800 year built from weekly double time, federal-only take-home is $60,044.80 for a single filer.
  • Check the written rule first: your handbook, contract, or state page decides whether double time exists for your job at all.

Sources & Method

The entitlement rules are stated from the Fair Labor Standards Act's overtime standard and U.S. Department of Labor guidance (a 1.5× federal floor past 40 hours a week, with no federal double-time, daily-overtime, or holiday premium), and from California Labor Code §510 with the California Department of Industrial Relations' overtime guidance (1.5× past 8 hours in a day and for the first 8 hours on a seventh consecutive workday; 2× past 12 hours in a day and past 8 hours on that seventh day). Premium pay is computed exactly as this site's overtime calculator computes it: regular, time-and-a-half, and double-time hours are priced separately at the regular rate × 1, × 1.5, and × 2, and no hour is priced twice. The after-tax sketch uses 2026 federal rules for a single filer taking the standard deduction: standard deduction $16,100, brackets 10% to $12,400, 12% to $50,400, 22% to $105,700 of taxable income, per IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-32; FICA 7.65% (Social Security 6.2% to the $184,500 wage base, Medicare 1.45%). State income tax, retirement contributions, and health premiums are excluded except where a note says otherwise. This article is general information, not legal or tax advice.

3 Things to Remember

  1. Double time pays 2× your regular rate, and only on hours past the trigger — never the whole shift.
  2. Federal law never grants it: California law, a union contract, or a written policy does.
  3. Double-time pay is taxed as ordinary wages — there is no special rate and no stacking with other premiums.

Methodology & Data Verification

  • Basis: Pay figures are gross unless a section states take-home; tax figures use 2026 federal rules where shown.
  • Method: Full formulas, baselines, and rounding rules are on our calculation methodology page.
  • Coverage: U.S. federal rules; state and local rules vary and are not included.
  • Review: Last updated October 29, 2026.
